memoryText: But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Isaiah 40:31 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse comes at the end of a long argument. The exiles in Babylon had said, “My way is hidden from the LORD.” Isaiah answers with a series of reasons to hope: the LORD is the Creator, never weary, whose understanding no one can fathom. And then comes the promise.

“But they who wait for the LORD.” The Hebrew word for wait does not mean to sit idly. It means to hope, to look expectantly, as a person watches for the dawn. It has the sense of being bound to someone, twisted together like a rope. To wait for the LORD is to tie your hope to him. This is not passive. It is a posture of active trust.

“Shall renew their strength.” The word “renew” means exchange. We trade our strength for his. The previous verses say that even the young grow faint and weary, and young men fall exhausted. Human strength has limits. But those who wait on God exchange their exhaustion for his inexhaustible power.

Then three pictures, in an unusual order. “They shall mount up with wings like eagles.” This is the most dramatic. “They shall run and not be weary.” This is steadier. “They shall walk and not faint.” This is the most ordinary, and perhaps the greatest miracle. Most of life is walking, not soaring. The promise is that God will sustain us in the daily grind as well as in the heights.

Say this verse in a time of fatigue. You may not feel like an eagle today. You may only be walking. The promise is that you will not faint, for you are leaning on the one who “does not faint or grow weary” (Isaiah 40:28).
weekInReview: This week you stood with Judah as Jerusalem celebrated its deliverance from Assyria, singing Psalms 46 and 48, with their refrain, “The LORD of hosts is with us,” and their command, “Be still, and know that I am God.” Then you crossed the great divide in the book of Isaiah. In chapters 40 to 42, God speaks comfort to exiles, prepares a highway in the wilderness, and introduces the Servant who will not break a bruised reed. In chapters 43 to 45, you heard the LORD claim his people by name, declare that there is no savior besides him, and name Cyrus as his shepherd. You prayed Psalm 86, a prayer of the poor and needy to a God who is good and forgiving, and Psalm 89, a song about the covenant God swore to David. The week taught that God comforts his people, that he is the only God, and that his covenant promises stand.
reflectionQuestions: Isaiah 40 begins, “Comfort, comfort my people.” Where do you most need to hear God’s comfort right now?
The Servant of Isaiah 42 does not break a bruised reed. How does Jesus’ gentleness with the weak change how you approach him in your own weakness?
God says, “I have called you by name, you are mine.” What difference would it make today if you lived as someone who truly belongs to him?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give power to the faint, and tell him where you are faint.
Thank him for the Servant who does not break a bruised reed.
Wait for him and ask him to renew your strength.
